issues.legal_issue: A magistrate may appoint an advocate as a commissioner to carry out the ministerial task of taking possession of secured assets and related documents and forwarding them to the secured creditor.
material_facts: Secured creditors sought magistrates’ assistance to take physical possession of secured assets after borrowers defaulted and did not repay despite demands.
The magistrates made possession orders and appointed advocates to carry them out by taking possession of the assets and related documents and forwarding them to the secured creditors.
The appointment question arose in proceedings challenging the magistrates’ authority to appoint advocates for that limited task.
issues.conclusion: A District Magistrate or Chief Metropolitan Magistrate may appoint an advocate commissioner to assist in executing an order for possession by taking possession of secured assets and related documents and forwarding them to the secured creditor.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13(4) and 14(1), (1A), (2) and (3) of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, read with Rule 8 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, permit the magistrate to use assistance in carrying out the ministerial step of taking possession. Section 14(1A) explains the magistrate’s existing power to use subordinate assistance; it does not expressly or by necessary implication exclude an advocate. Applying functional subordination, the Court held that an advocate, as an officer of the court, is subordinate to the magistrate for this limited function, even though the advocate is not part of the magistrate’s administrative or statutory hierarchy. The Court relied on the reasoning in Muhammed Ashraf and Sakiri Vasu concerning implied powers to make statutory authority effective, and on Lalit Mohan Das and O.P. Sharma concerning advocates’ duties as officers of the court. A. St. Arunachalam Pillai was considered in distinguishing administrative subordination. The Court held that the contrary strict-interpretation judgment was not good law and upheld the consistent view of the other High Courts.

rule.if: secured_loan_enforcement_proceeding and magistrate_received_possession_request and possession_order_requires_execution and advocate_is_court_officer and task_is_only_ministerial_possession and no_rule_excludes_advocate

predicates.secured_loan_enforcement_proceeding: A secured creditor pursued a process to enforce a security interest and obtain possession of secured property.
predicates.magistrate_received_possession_request: The secured creditor asked a magistrate to arrange for possession of the secured property and related documents.
predicates.possession_order_requires_execution: The magistrate made an order after which the property and related documents had to be taken and forwarded to the secured creditor.
predicates.advocate_is_court_officer: The person considered for the task was an advocate who serves as an officer of the court.
predicates.task_is_only_ministerial_possession: The advocate’s assigned task was limited to carrying out possession and forwarding the property and related documents, rather than deciding disputed rights.
predicates.no_rule_excludes_advocate: No applicable rule expressly or by necessary implication barred the magistrate from engaging an advocate for that limited task.

issues.definition: When a secured creditor seeks possession through a magistrate, the magistrate has made an order requiring possession to be carried out, an advocate who is an officer of the court is assigned only the ministerial possession task, and no applicable rule excludes that assistance, the magistrate may appoint the advocate commissioner.
